text: You already know the mechanics from course 2 — tables, the dictionary, field types, and extending an existing base table instead of starting from nothing. This lesson is about the architecture decision underneath those mechanics: what happens to a table design once it's carrying real production volume for years, not a thousand test records.

Every field adds a column, and width isn't free. A table with 40 fields, 15 of them rarely populated, is still a wider row than a lean table — even for a query that only touches three fields, because row storage doesn't care which columns the query actually asked for. Every indexed field also adds write overhead on every insert and update, forever, not just once. None of this shows up in a dev instance with 500 records. It only shows up in production, years later.

Course 2 taught table extension as a mechanic — extend task and inherit its fields. At architecture scale, that choice carries real weight both ways. Extend the base table when the new data genuinely is a kind of task, and you're willing to accept that the shared table gets a little wider every time. Build a new, unrelated table when the data doesn't semantically belong there, or you want to isolate its growth from task's own volume. There's no universal right answer — and the wrong call is expensive to undo once a dozen reports and integrations assume the current structure.

The real discipline is asking, at design time, what this table looks like after eight years of real use. Prefer reference fields over long free-text fields for categorical data, since reference fields index and filter far better at volume. Resist adding a field just in case it's useful later — every field is permanent width the table carries forever, whether or not it's ever used. And design around how the table will actually be queried and reported on, before it's built, not around what fields seemed natural to add.

Field count, table width, and the extend-versus-build-new decision are the foundation of sound table design at scale. Next up: what happens to that design after years of accumulated records — a real archiving strategy.
